Logarithmic estimates for mean-field models in dimension two and the Schrödinger-Poisson system

Jean Dolbeault Address: J. Dolbeault: CEREMADE (CNRS UMR n∘ 7534), PSL university, Université Paris-Dauphine
Place de Lattre de Tassigny, 75775 Paris 16, France Email address: dolbeaul@ceremade.dauphine.fr , Rupert L. Frank Address: R.L. Frank: Mathematisches Institut, Ludwig-Maximilans Universität München, Theresienstr. 39, 80333 München, Germany, and Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology, Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany, and Mathematics 253-37, Caltech, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA Email address: r.frank@lmu.de and Louis Jeanjean Address: L. Jeanjean: Laboratoire de Mathématiques (CNRS UMR n∘ 6623), Université of Bourgogne Franche-Comté, 25030 Besançon Cedex, France Email address: louis.jeanjean@univ-fcomte.fr
Date: August 24, 2026. File: log-Poisson-2.tex
Abstract.

In dimension two, we investigate a free energy and the ground state energy of the Schrödinger-Poisson system coupled with a logarithmic nonlinearity in terms of underlying functional inequalities which take into account the scaling invariances of the problem. Such a system can be considered as a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a cubic but nonlocal Poisson nonlinearity, and a local logarithmic nonlinearity. Both cases of repulsive and attractive forces are considered. We also assume that there is an external potential with minimal growth at infinity, which turns out to have a logarithmic growth. Our estimates rely on new logarithmic interpolation inequalities which combine logarithmic Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. The two-dimensional model appears as a limit case of more classical problems in higher dimensions.

Key words and phrases: 
Schrödinger-Poisson system; nonlinear Schrödinger equation; mean-field coupling; Poisson equation; Newton equation; interpolation; logarithmic Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality; logarithmic Sobolev inequality
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
35J50; 35Q55; 35J47

1. The Schrödinger-Poisson system with a local logarithmic nonlinearity

The standard Schrödinger-Poisson (SP) system is a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with cubic but nonlocal nonlinearity. As for the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation with a local nonlinearity, scaling properties play a crucial role in the analysis of the solutions and depend on the dimension dd of the Euclidean space. The fact that the nonlinearity in (SP) involves the Poisson convolution kernel makes existence results easier to study than for (NLS) because of the compactness properties induced by the convolution, but adds difficulties due to the non-locality of the mean field potential. We consider primarily the case d=2d=2.

Our purpose is to focus on the underlying functional inequalities and study the interaction of the Poisson term with other terms in the energy (external potential, local nonlinearities) with similar scaling properties: we shall consider quantities which are all critical for (SP) in the two-dimensional case. This is quite interesting from the mathematical point of view, as it is a threshold case for (SP) systems and involves a non sign-defined logarithmic kernel. The d=2d=2 case complements the results of [17, 18] in the limit regime involving logarithmic local nonlinearities. For related questions for d=3d=3, we refer to [17] and references therein. In higher dimensions, the problem is sub-critical if d≤5d\leq 5 and critical for d=6d=6: see Section 3.2.

The (SP) system is used in quantum mechanics to represent a large number of particles by a single complex valued wave function. The local nonlinear term arises from local effects or thermodynamical considerations while the non-local Poisson potential accounts for long range forces which are either of repulsive nature (charged particles) or attractive (in case of gravitational and related models). Most models in the physics literature are justified only on an empirical basis as thermodynamical limits but are difficult to establish rigorously. This issue is anyway out of the scope of this paper.

The Schrödinger equation with a logarithmic nonlinearity is a remarkable model in physics, with interesting mathematical properties: see [5, 12, 34]. The equation has soliton-like solutions of Gaussian shape (called Gaussons in [5]). We shall refer to [16, 14, 15, 20] for some additional contributions in mathematics. Schrödinger-Poisson systems are commonly used in charged particles transport and particularly in semiconductor physics, in the repulsive case. In this direction, a classical reference for mathematical properties is [13] and we also quote [4, 36] for examples of applications. The mean-field attractive case (Newton equation) reflects gravitational forces instead of electrostatic forces. It is not studied as much as the repulsive case and it is mathematically more difficult: see for instance [36, Section 4]. As a side remark, we may notice that stationary solutions of (SP) share many properties with stationary solutions of two-dimensional models of chemotaxis, and the same functional inequalities are involved: see [24]. We can however handle the two cases, attractive and repulsive, in a common framework. We primarily focus on variational results, in relation with some interesting functional inequalities and their scaling properties.

For any function u∈H1​(ℝ2)u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), let us consider the Schrödinger energy

ℰ⁡[u]:=∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x+α​∫ℝ2V​|u|2​𝑑x+2​π​β​∫ℝ2W​|u|2​𝑑x+γ​∫ℝ2|u|2​log​|u|2​𝑑x\mathcal{E}[u]:=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx+\alpha\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{V\,|u|^{2}}\,dx+2\,\pi\,\beta\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{W\,|u|^{2}}\,dx+\gamma\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,\log|u|^{2}}\,dx (1)

where α\alpha, β\beta, γ\gamma are real parameters and the self-consistent potential WW is obtained as a solution of the Poisson equation

−Δ​W=|u|2.-\,\Delta W=|u|^{2}\,.

The solution WW of (1) is defined only up to an additive constant: we make the specific choice W=(−Δ)−1​|u|2W=(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2} given by the Green kernel as follows. Let us recall that on ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} the standard Green function GyG_{y} associated with (−Δ)(-\Delta), that is, the solution of −Δx​G=δy​(x)-\Delta_{x}G=\delta_{y}(x), is given by

G⁡(x,y)=−12​π​log⁡|x−y|∀(x,y)∈ℝ2×ℝ2.G(x,y)=-\,\frac{1}{2\,\pi}\,\log|x-y|\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,(x,y)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\,.

Our choice amounts to take W⁡(x)=∫ℝ2|u⁡(y)|2​G​(x,y)​𝑑yW(x)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}|u(y)|^{2}\,G(x,y)\,dy. As a consequence, we have

W⁡(x)∼−‖u‖222​π​log⁡|x|as|x|→+∞,W(x)\sim-\,\frac{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2\,\pi}\,\log|x|\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{as}\hskip 10.00002pt|x|\to+\infty\,,

and also x⋅∇W​(x)<0x\cdot\nabla W(x)<0 for large values of |x||x| if, for instance, uu is compactly supported. The cases β>0\beta>0 and β<0\beta<0 correspond to two very different physical situations. The case β<0\beta<0 is the attractive case of a Newton-Poisson coupling for gravitational mean-field models. With β>0\beta>0, the model represents the two-dimensional case of repulsive electrostatic forces, i.e., a mean field version of a quantum Coulomb gas of interacting particles in dimension d=2d=2.

The function VV is an external potential, and we shall assume that it has a critical growth. The parameter α∈ℝ\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}} is a coupling parameter, whose value has to be discussed depending on the other terms. Without much loss of generality, we can assume that

V⁡(x)=2​log⁡(1+|x|2)∀x∈ℝ2.V(x)=2\,\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\,. (2)

Concerning the local nonlinearity, the case γ<0\gamma<0 corresponds to a focusing local nonlinearity while γ>0\gamma>0 is the case a defocusing local nonlinearity. It is standard to observe that any critical point of ℰ\mathcal{E} under the mass constraint

∫ℝ2|u|2​𝑑x=M\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}}\,dx=M

determines a standing wave of the nonlinear Schrödinger-Poisson system

i​∂ψ∂t=Δ​ψ+α​V​ψ+β​W​ψ+γ​log⁡|ψ|2​ψ.i\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}=\Delta\psi+\alpha\,V\,\psi+\beta\,W\,\psi+\,\gamma\,\log|\psi|^{2}\,\psi\,.

In this paper we shall focus on finding conditions on α\alpha, β\beta, γ∈ℝ\gamma\in{\mathbb{R}} insuring that the functional ℰ\mathcal{E} is either bounded or unbounded from below on

ℋM:={u∈H1​(ℝ2):‖u‖22=M}.\mathcal{H}_{M}:=\left\{u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\,:\,\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}=M\right\}\,.

This paper is organized as follows. We establish in Section 2 several new functional inequalities which generalize the logarithmic Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality, with an application to a free energy functional in dimension two: see Theorem 3. Section 3 is devoted to the boundedness from below of the Schrödinger energy ℰ\mathcal{E}, with main results in Theorem 10.

2. New logarithmic inequalities and free energy estimates

2.1. Generalized logarithmic Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequalities

The logarithmic Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality

∫ℝ2ρ​log⁡(ρM)​𝑑x+2M​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log​|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y+M⁡(1+log⁡π)≥0\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho\,\log\left(\frac{\rho}{M}\right)}\,dx+\frac{2}{M}\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy+M\,(1+\log\pi)\geq 0 (3)

has been established in optimal form in [11] by E. Carlen and M. Loss, and in [1] by W. Beckner for any ρ∈L+1​(ℝ2)\rho\in\mathrm{L}^{1}_{+}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) such that ∫ℝ2ρ​𝑑x=M>0\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho}\,dx=M>0. Equality is achieved by ρ=ρ⋆\rho=\rho_{\star} with

ρ⋆​(x):=Mπ​(1+|x|2)2∀x∈ℝ2,\rho_{\star}(x):=\frac{M}{\pi\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)^{2}}\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\,, (4)

and also by any function obtained from ρ⋆\rho_{\star} by a multiplication by a positive constant (with the corresponding mass constraint), a scaling or a translation. Alternative proofs based on fast diffusion flows have been obtained in [10, 21, 23]. Also see [2, 7, 22, 35] for further related results and considerations on dual Onofri type inequalities and [28] for a rearrangement-free proof of (3) using reflection positivity. Inequality (3) provides us with a useful lower bound on the free energy in the case of an attractive Poisson equation corresponding to the Keller-Segel model: see [6, 25], or in the case of a mean-field Newton equation in gravitational models. In presence of the potential VV given by (2), we have

∫ℝ2ρ​log⁡(ρM)​dx+2​τ​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​dx+M⁡(1−τ+log⁡π)≥2M​(τ−1)​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log⁡|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho\,\log\left(\frac{\rho}{M}\right)}\,dx+2\,\tau\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx+M\,(1-\tau+\log\pi)\\ \geq\frac{2}{M}\,(\tau-1)\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy (5)

for any τ≥0\tau\geq 0 and for any function ρ∈L+1​(ℝ2)\rho\in\mathrm{L}^{1}_{+}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) with M=∫ℝ2ρ​𝑑x>0M=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho}\,dx>0, according to [24]. Compared to [24], the discrepancy in the coefficient of MM in the last term of the r.h.s. in (5) is due to the normalization of VV as defined by (2). Equality again holds if ρ=ρ⋆\rho=\rho_{\star} given by (4). When τ=0\tau=0, (5) is nothing else than (3) while the case τ=1\tau=1 is easily recovered by Jensen’s inequality. Notice that the sign of the coefficient in front of the convolution term in the r.h.s. of (5) becomes positive if τ>1\tau>1.

Let us divide (5) by τ>0\tau>0 and then take the limit as τ→+∞\tau\to+\infty. By doing this, we obtain a new inequality, which differs from (3) and is of interest by itself.

Lemma 1.

For any function ρ∈L+1​(ℝ2)\rho\in\mathrm{L}^{1}_{+}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) such that ∫ℝ2ρ​𝑑x=M\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho}\,dx=M, we have

2​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x−M≥2M​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log​|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y.2\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx-M\geq\frac{2}{M}\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy\,. (6)

Moreover equality in (6) is achieved if and only if ρ=ρ⋆\rho=\rho_{\star}.

Proof.

We give a direct proof of (6), which does not rely on (5). A preliminary observation is that (6) makes sense, i.e., that

ρ↦∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x−1M​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log​|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y\rho\mapsto\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx-\frac{1}{M}\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy

is bounded from below. We may indeed notice that, for any xx, y∈ℝdy\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},

|x−y|2=|x|2+|y|2−2​x⋅y≤|x|2+|y|2+(1+|x|2​|y|2)=(1+|x|2)​(1+|y|2),|x-y|^{2}=|x|^{2}+|y|^{2}-2\,x\cdot y\leq|x|^{2}+|y|^{2}+\left(1+|x|^{2}\,|y|^{2}\right)=\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\left(1+|y|^{2}\right)\,,

so that, after multiplying by ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)\rho(x)\,\rho(y) and integrating with respect to xx and yy, we obtain

2​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log⁡|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y\displaystyle 2\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy
≤∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​(log⁡(1+|x|2)+log⁡(1+|y|2))​𝑑x​𝑑y≤2​M​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x.\displaystyle\leq\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\Big(\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)+\log\left(1+|y|^{2}\right)\Big)\,dx\,dy\leq 2\,M\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx\,.

As a consequence, the problem is reduced to proving that the largest constant CC such that

2​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x−C≥2M​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log​|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y2\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx-C\geq\frac{2}{M}\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy

is C=MC=M.

At heuristic level, if we admit that ρ⋆\rho_{\star} realizes the equality case, this equality can be established as follows. The potential VV given by (2) is such that μ⋆=1π​e−V=ρ⋆M\mu_{\star}=\frac{1}{\pi}\,e^{-V}=\frac{\rho_{\star}}{M} is a probability measure and we have

Δ​V=8​π​μ⋆.\Delta V=8\,\pi\,\mu_{\star}\,.

One can also check that

(−Δ)−1μ⋆:=−12​π∫ℝ2log|x−y|μ⋆(y)dy=−V8​π=−14​πlog(1+|x|2)(-\Delta)^{-1}\mu_{\star}:=-\frac{1}{2\,\pi}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\log|x-y|\,\mu_{\star}(y)\,dy=-\,\frac{V}{8\,\pi}=-\,\frac{1}{4\,\pi}\,\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)

which requires a careful analysis of the integration constants. Indeed, in radial coordinates, by solving the ordinary differential equation

(r​V′)′=8​r(1+r2),V′​(0)=0,V⁡(0)=V0,\big(r\,V^{\prime}\big)^{\prime}=\frac{8\,r}{\left(1+r^{2}\right)}\,,\hskip 10.00002ptV^{\prime}(0)=0\,,\hskip 10.00002ptV(0)=V_{0}\,,

a couple of integrations shows that

V′​(r)=1r​(41+r2−4)andV⁡(r)−V0=∫0r4​s1+s2​𝑑s=2​log⁡(1+r2),V^{\prime}(r)=\frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{4}{1+r^{2}}-4\right)\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002ptV(r)-V_{0}=\int_{0}^{r}\frac{4\,s}{1+s^{2}}\,ds=2\,\log\left(1+r^{2}\right)\,,

so that 8​π​(−Δ)−1​μ⋆=−(V+V0)8\,\pi\,(-\Delta)^{-1}\mu_{\star}=-(V+V_{0}) with V0=0V_{0}=0. Alternatively, a direct proof is obtained by observing that

V0=4​∫ℝ2log⁡|y|​μ⋆​(y)​𝑑y=8​∫0+∞r​log⁡r(1+r2)2​𝑑r=0,V_{0}=4\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\log|y|\,\mu_{\star}(y)\,dy=8\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{r\,\log r}{\left(1+r^{2}\right)^{2}}\,dr=0\,,

where the last equality is a consequence of the change of variables r↦1/rr\mapsto 1/r. Taking into account the identity

∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​μ⋆​(x)​𝑑x=∫0+∞2​r​log⁡(1+r2)(1+r2)2​𝑑r=1,\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\,\mu_{\star}(x)}\,dx=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{2\,r\,\log\left(1+r^{2}\right)}{\left(1+r^{2}\right)^{2}}\,dr=1\,,

this is consistent with the fact that ρ⋆=M​μ⋆\rho_{\star}=M\,\mu_{\star} corresponds to the equality case in (3), according to [11]. Altogether, we have C=MC=M, meaning that (6) is an equality if ρ=ρ⋆\rho=\rho_{\star}.

After these preliminary considerations, which are provided only for a better understanding of the functional framework, let us give a proof. With no loss of generality, we may assume that M=1M=1 because of the 11-homogeneity of (6). Let us notice that

2​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x−1−2​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log​|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y=− 2∬ℝ2×ℝ2(ρ(x)−μ⋆(x))(ρ(y)−μ⋆(y))log|x−y|dxdy.2\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx-1-2\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy\\ =-\,2\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\big(\rho(x)-\mu_{\star}(x)\big)\,\big(\rho(y)-\mu_{\star}(y)\big)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy.

We recover that the equality case in (6) is achieved if ρ=μ⋆\rho=\mu_{\star}. With W=−(−Δ)−1​(ρ−μ⋆)W=-(-\Delta)^{-1}(\rho-\mu_{\star}), we obtain

− 2∬ℝ2×ℝ2(ρ(x)−μ⋆(x))(ρ(y)−μ⋆(y))log|x−y|dxdy=4​π​∫ℝ2(ρ−μ⋆)​(−Δ)−1​(ρ−μ⋆)​𝑑x=− 4π∫ℝ2(ΔW)Wdx=4π∫ℝ2|∇W|2dx≥0,-\,2\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\big(\rho(x)-\mu_{\star}(x)\big)\,\big(\rho(y)-\mu_{\star}(y)\big)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy\\ =4\,\pi\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{(\rho-\mu_{\star})\,(-\Delta)^{-1}(\rho-\mu_{\star})}\,dx\\ =-\,4\,\pi\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{(\Delta W)\,W}\,dx=4\,\pi\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla W|^{2}}\,dx\geq 0\,,

where the last equality is obtained by a simple integration by parts. This can be done only because ∫ℝ2(ρ−μ⋆)​𝑑x=0\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{(\rho-\mu_{\star})}\,dx=0, a necessary and sufficient condition to guarantee that ∇W\nabla W is square integrable (for a proof, one has to study the behavior of the solution of the Poisson equation as |x|→+∞|x|\to+\infty). At this point it is clear that ∫ℝ2|∇W|2​𝑑x=0\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla W|^{2}}\,dx=0 if and only if ρ=μ⋆\rho=\mu_{\star}. The general case with an arbitrary M>0M>0 is obtained by writing ρ⋆=M​μ⋆\rho_{\star}=M\;\mu_{\star}, which concludes the proof. ∎

The equality case in (6) is achieved among radial functions. It is classical that the l.h.s. is decreasing under symmetric decreasing rearrangements, while the r.h.s. is increasing. The strict rearrangement inequality for the logarithmic kernel is proved in [11, Lemma 2]. As a limit case of ∬ℝ2×ℝ2(ρ⁡(x)−μ⋆​(x))​(ρ⁡(y)−μ⋆​(y))​|x−y|λ​𝑑x​𝑑y\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\big(\rho(x)-\mu_{\star}(x)\big)\,\big(\rho(y)-\mu_{\star}(y)\big)\,|x-y|^{\lambda}\,dx\,dy when λ→0−\lambda\to 0_{-}, according to [30, Theorem 4.3] (also see [33] for interesting consequences), this is indeed expected. Justifying the square integrability of ∇W\nabla W has therefore to be done only among radial functions, which is elementary using, e.g., a compactly supported function ρ\rho and a density argument.

Also notice that one can now recover (5) as a simple consequence of (3) and (6). Next, we turn our attention to an inequality which is a consequence of convexity and Jensen’s inequality. Let

𝖩η​[ρ]:=∫ℝ2ρ​log⁡(ρ‖ρ‖1)​𝑑x+η​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x∀ρ∈L+1​(ℝ2).\mathsf{J}_{\eta}[\rho]:=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho\,\log\left(\frac{\rho}{\left\|{\rho}\right\|_{1}}\right)}\,dx+\eta\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,\rho\in\mathrm{L}^{1}_{+}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\,.
Lemma 2.

Let η>0\eta>0, M>0M>0 and 𝒳M:={ρ∈L+1​(ℝ2):‖ρ‖1=M}\mathcal{X}_{M}:=\left\{\rho\in\mathrm{L}^{1}_{+}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\,:\,\left\|{\rho}\right\|_{1}=M\right\}.

  1. (i)

    If η>1\eta>1, then 𝖩η\mathsf{J}_{\eta} is bounded from below on 𝒳M\mathcal{X}_{M} and

    ∫ℝ2ρ​log⁡(ρM)​𝑑x+η​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x≥M​log⁡(η−1π)∀ρ∈𝒳M.\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho\,\log\left(\frac{\rho}{M}\right)}\,dx+\eta\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx\geq M\,\log\Big(\frac{\eta-1}{\pi}\Big)\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,\rho\in\mathcal{X}_{M}\,. (7)

    For any η>1\eta>1, equality in (7) is achieved by ρ=M​ρη\rho=M\,\rho_{\eta}, where

    ρη​(x):=η−1π​(1+|x|2)η∀x∈ℝ2.\rho_{\eta}(x):=\frac{\eta-1}{\pi\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)^{\eta}}\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\,.
  2. (ii)

    If η∈(0,1]\eta\in(0,1], then inf𝒳M𝖩η=−∞\inf_{\mathcal{X}_{M}}\mathsf{J}_{\eta}=-\infty.

If η=2\eta=2, then ρ2=ρ⋆\rho_{2}=\rho_{\star}, while (7) amounts to 𝖩η​[ρ]≥𝖩η​[M​ρη]\mathsf{J}_{\eta}[\rho]\geq\mathsf{J}_{\eta}[M\,\rho_{\eta}] for any η>1\eta>1. If τ\tau is restricted to the range [0,1][0,1], we notice as in [24] that (5) is a simple convex combination, with coefficients (1−τ)(1-\tau) and τ\tau, of (3) and (7) written with η=2\eta=2.

Proof.

A direct computation based on dd​r​(1+r2)1−η=−2​(η−1)​r​(1+r2)−η\frac{d}{dr}\left(1+r^{2}\right)^{1-\eta}=-2\,(\eta-1)\,r\left(1+r^{2}\right)^{-\eta} shows that

∫ℝ2ρη​𝑑x=2​(η−1)​∫0+∞r​(1+r2)−η​𝑑r=1\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho_{\eta}}\,dx=2\,(\eta-1)\int_{0}^{+\infty}r\left(1+r^{2}\right)^{-\eta}\,dr=1

for all η>1\eta>1 and

2.2. Boundedness from below of the free energy functional

Let us consider the free energy functional defined by

for some constant 𝒞⁡(𝖺,𝖻)\mathcal{C}(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}). Inequality (5) with τ≥0\tau\geq 0 is obtained as the special case 𝖺=2​τ\mathsf{a}=2\,\tau and 𝖻=2​(τ−1)\mathsf{b}=2\,(\tau-1), with 𝒞⁡(𝖺,𝖻)=M⁡(τ−1−log⁡π)\mathcal{C}(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b})=M\,(\tau-1-\log\pi), according to [24]. As a consequence, we also know that (8) holds for some 𝒞⁡(𝖺,𝖻)>−∞\mathcal{C}(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b})>-\infty if 𝖺≥2​τ\mathsf{a}\geq 2\,\tau and 𝖻=2​(τ−1)\mathsf{b}=2\,(\tau-1), that is, 0≤𝖻+2≤𝖺0\leq\mathsf{b}+2\leq\mathsf{a}. The proof of Theorem 3 in the case 𝖻=2(𝖺−1)∈[−2,0)\mathsf{b}=2\,(\mathsf{a}-1)\in[-2,0) is based on two ingredients exposed in Lemma 6 and Lemma 7. Let 0≤𝖺<10\leq\mathsf{a}<1. Then

Let σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 with ∫ℝ2σ​𝑑x=1\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\sigma\,dx=1 and with compact support not containing the origin. Consider ρλ​(x)=λ−2​σ​(x/λ)\rho_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda^{-2}\sigma(x/\lambda) with λ≫1\lambda\gg 1. Then, as in the proof of Lemma 5,

ℱ𝖺,𝖻​[ρλ]=(−2+2​𝖺−𝖻)​log⁡λ+∫ℝ2σlogσdx+𝖺∫ℝ2log(λ−2+|x|2)σ(x)dx+𝖻∬ℝ2×ℝ2σ(x)log1|x−y|σ(y)dxdy.\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}[\rho_{\lambda}]=(-2+2\,\mathsf{a}-\mathsf{b})\log\lambda\\ +\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\sigma\,\log\sigma\,dx+\mathsf{a}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\log\left(\lambda^{-2}+|x|^{2}\right)\sigma(x)\,dx\\ +\mathsf{b}\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\sigma(x)\,\log\frac{1}{|x-y|}\,\sigma(y)\,dx\,dy\,.

Taking the infimum over all σ\sigma (and removing the support assumptions by an approximation argument), we obtain 𝒞⁡(𝖺,2​(𝖺−1))≤𝒦⁡(𝖺)\mathcal{C}\big(\mathsf{a},2\,(\mathsf{a}-1)\big)\leq\mathcal{K}(\mathsf{a}), as claimed. ∎

Lemma 7.

Let 0≤𝖺<10\leq\mathsf{a}<1. Then

𝒦⁡(𝖺)=−log⁡(e​π1−𝖺).\mathcal{K}(\mathsf{a})=-\log\left(\frac{e\,\pi}{1-\mathsf{a}}\right)\,.

For 𝖺>0\mathsf{a}>0 the infimum 𝒦⁡(𝖺)\mathcal{K}(\mathsf{a}) is achieved if and only if, for some λ>0\lambda>0,

2.3. Additional remarks on the free energy and some open questions

In Lemma 4, Inequality (8) holds for some finite constant 𝒞⁡(𝖺,𝖻)\mathcal{C}(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}) if (𝖺,𝖻)=(0,−2)(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b})=(0,-2) . We also know from Lemma 2 that lim𝖺→1+𝒞⁡(𝖺,0)=−∞\lim_{\mathsf{a}\to 1_{+}}\mathcal{C}(\mathsf{a},0)=-\infty. If 𝖻=𝖺−1>0\mathsf{b}=\mathsf{a}-1>0, it is so far open to decide whether (8) holds for some 𝒞⁡(𝖺,𝖻)>−∞\mathcal{C}(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b})>-\infty. See Fig. 1.

The free energy ℱ𝖺,𝖻​[ρ]\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}[\rho] is a natural Lyapunov functional for the drift-diffusion equation

∂ρ∂t=Δρ+∇⋅(ρ(𝖺∇V+4π𝖻M∇W)),W=(−Δ)−1ρ.\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}=\Delta\rho+\nabla\cdot\Big(\rho\,\big(\mathsf{a}\,\nabla V+4\,\pi\,\tfrac{\mathsf{b}}{M}\,\nabla W\big)\Big)\,,\hskip 10.00002ptW=(-\Delta)^{-1}\rho\,. (9)

Indeed we can write that Δρ=∇⋅(ρ∇logρ)\Delta\rho=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho\,\nabla\log\rho\right) so that, for any smooth and sufficiently decreasing function ρ\rho solving (9), we obtain using an integration by parts that

dd​tℱ𝖺,𝖻[ρ(t,⋅)]=−∫ℝ2ρ|∇logρ+𝖺∇V+4π𝖻M∇W|2dx.\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}[\rho(t,\cdot)]=-\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho\,\left|\nabla\log\rho+\mathsf{a}\,\nabla V+4\,\pi\,\tfrac{\mathsf{b}}{M}\,\nabla W\right|^{2}}\,dx\,.

Concerning the the long time behavior of the solution of (9), we expect that ℱ𝖺,𝖻​[ρ​(t,⋅)]\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}[\rho(t,\cdot)] converges to 𝒞⁡(𝖺,𝖻)\mathcal{C}(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}) as t→+∞t\to+\infty by analogy, e.g., with the Keller-Segel system (see [6, Section 4]), but it is an open question to deduce global decay rates of ℱ𝖺,𝖻​[ρ​(t,⋅)]\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}[\rho(t,\cdot)], for instance in a restricted class of solutions of (9), or even asymptotic decay rates as in [8]. Another issue is to understand the counterpart on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} of the results on ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} using the inverse stereographic projection, as in [11, 21, 23].

For any M>0M>0, the boundedness from below of

ℱ𝖺,𝖻𝖼​[ρ]:=𝖺​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρ​𝑑x−𝖻M​∬ℝ2×ℝ2ρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)​log|x−y|d​x​𝑑y+𝖼​∫ℝ2ρ​log⁡(ρM)​𝑑x\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}^{\,\mathsf{c}}[\rho]:=\mathsf{a}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\!\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho}\,dx-\frac{\mathsf{b}}{M}\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\!\rho(x)\,\rho(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy+\mathsf{c}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\!\rho\,\log\left(\frac{\rho}{M}\right)}\,dx

on the set 𝒳M\mathcal{X}_{M} arises for any 𝖼>0\mathsf{c}>0 as a straightforward consequence of Lemma 4 under the obvious condition − 2​𝖼≤𝖻<min⁡{𝖺−𝖼,2​𝖺−2​𝖼}-\,2\,\mathsf{c}\leq\mathsf{b}<\min\{\mathsf{a}-\mathsf{c},2\,\mathsf{a}-2\,\mathsf{c}\}, by homogeneity. The case 𝖼=0\mathsf{c}=0 is covered by Lemma 1. It is therefore a natural question to inquire what happens if 𝖼<0\mathsf{c}<0.

Proposition 8.

For any (𝖺,𝖻)∈ℝ2(\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} and M>0M>0, with the above notations, if 𝖼<0\mathsf{c}<0, then

infρ∈𝒳Mℱ𝖺,𝖻𝖼​[ρ]=−∞.\inf_{\rho\,\in\mathcal{X}_{M}}\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}^{\,\mathsf{c}}[\rho]=-\infty\,.
Proof.

The key point of the proof is that ρ↦𝖼​∫ℝ2ρ​log⁡ρ​𝑑x\rho\mapsto\mathsf{c}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho\,\log\rho}\,dx with 𝖼<0\mathsf{c}<0 is a concave functional. Let ρ∈𝒳1\rho\in\mathcal{X}_{1} be a function supported in the unit ball. For any ε∈(0,1/4)\varepsilon\in(0,1/4) and n∈ℕ∖{0}n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}, let

Rε,n​(x):=1n2​∑k,ℓ=1nε−2​ρ​(ε−1​(x−(k,ℓ)))∀x∈ℝ2.R_{\varepsilon,n}(x):=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}\varepsilon^{-2}\,\rho\left(\varepsilon^{-1}\,\big(x-(k,\ell)\big)\right)\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\,.

In order to investigate the limits ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0_{+} and n→+∞n\to+\infty, we compute

∫ℝ2Rε,n​log​Rε,n​𝑑x=−log⁡(n2​ε2)+∫ℝ2ρ​log​ρ​𝑑x=− 2​log⁡(n​ε)+O⁡(1),\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{R_{\varepsilon,n}\,\log R_{\varepsilon,n}}\,dx=-\,\log\left(n^{2}\,\varepsilon^{2}\right)+\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho\,\log\rho}\,dx=-\,2\,\log\left(n\,\varepsilon\right)+O(1)\,,
∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​Rε,n​𝑑x≲log⁡(1+2​n2)=2​log⁡n⁡(1+o⁡(1)),\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)R_{\varepsilon,n}}\,dx\lesssim\log\left(1+2\,n^{2}\right)=2\,\log n\,\big(1+o(1)\big)\,,
|∬ℝ2×ℝ2Rε,n​(x)​Rε,n​(y)​log⁡|x−y|​𝑑x​𝑑y|≲|log⁡ε|n2+log⁡(1+2​n2)2​n2\displaystyle\left|\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}R_{\varepsilon,n}(x)\,R_{\varepsilon,n}(y)\,\log|x-y|\,dx\,dy\right|\lesssim\frac{|\log\varepsilon|}{n^{2}}+\frac{\log\left(1+2\,n^{2}\right)}{2\,n^{2}}
=|log⁡(ε/n)|n2​(1+o​(1)).\displaystyle\hskip 284.52756pt=\frac{|\log(\varepsilon/n)|}{n^{2}}\,\big(1+o(1)\big)\,.

With the choice ε=n−A\varepsilon=n^{-A} for some A>0A>0 large enough, we find that 𝖼​∫ℝ2Rε,n​log⁡Rε,n​𝑑x∼(A−1)​|𝖼|​log⁡n→−∞\mathsf{c}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{R_{\varepsilon,n}\,\log R_{\varepsilon,n}}\,dx\sim(A-1)\,|\mathsf{c}|\,\log n\to-\infty as n→+∞n\to+\infty and this term dominates the other ones. This concludes the proof. ∎

3. Logarithmic interpolation inequalities and Schrödinger energy estimates

We are now going to study the Schrödinger energy ℰ\mathcal{E} defined by (1). As we shall see, the kinetic energy ∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx completely changes the picture and considering 𝖼<0\mathsf{c}<0 makes sense.

3.1. A new logarithmic interpolation inequality

Here we combine logarithmic Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequalities with the logarithmic Sobolev inequality to produce a new logarithmic interpolation inequality. This new inequality is more directly connected with the Schrödinger-Poisson system (SP).

In dimension d=2d=2, with the Gaussian measure defined as d​μ=μ⁡(x)​d​xd\mu=\mu(x)\,dx where μ(x)=(2π)−1exp(−|x|2/2)\mu(x)=(2\,\pi)^{-1}\,\exp(-|x|^{2}/2), the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality reads

∫ℝ2|∇v|2​𝑑μ≥12​∫ℝ2|v|2​log⁡|v|2​𝑑μ\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla v|^{2}}\,d\mu\geq\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|v|^{2}\,\log|v|^{2}}\,d\mu (10)

for any function v∈H1​(ℝ2,d​μ)v\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2},d\mu) such that ∫ℝ2|v|2​𝑑μ=1\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|v|^{2}}\,d\mu=1, and there is equality if and only if v≡1v\equiv 1 (see [9, Theorem 4]). With u=v​μu=v\,\sqrt{\mu}, it is a classical fact that Inequality (10) is equivalent to the standard Euclidean logarithmic Sobolev inequality established in [29] (also see [27] for an earlier related result) which can be written in dimension d=2d=2 as

∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x≥12​∫ℝ2|u|2​log⁡(|u|2‖u‖22)​𝑑x+12​log⁡(2​π​e2)​‖u‖22\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx\geq\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,\log\left(\frac{|u|^{2}}{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\right)}\,dx+\frac{1}{2}\,\log\left(2\,\pi\,e^{2}\right)\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2} (11)

for any function u∈H1​(ℝ2,d​x)u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2},dx). This inequality is not invariant under scaling. By applying (11) to the scaled function uλ​(x)=λ​u​(λ​x)u_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda\,u(\lambda\,x), we obtain

λ2​‖∇u‖22−log⁡λ​‖u‖22≥12​∫ℝ2|u|2​log⁡(|u|2‖u‖22)​𝑑x+12​log⁡(2​π​e2)​‖u‖22\lambda^{2}\,\left\|{\nabla u}\right\|_{2}^{2}-\log\lambda\,\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,\log\left(\frac{|u|^{2}}{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\right)}\,dx+\frac{1}{2}\,\log\left(2\,\pi\,e^{2}\right)\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2} (12)

for any λ>0\lambda>0. The scaling parameter λ\lambda can be optimized in order to obtain the Euclidean logarithmic Sobolev inequality in scale invariant form

‖u‖22​log⁡(1π​e​‖∇u‖22‖u‖22)≥∫ℝ2|u|2​log⁡(|u|2‖u‖22)​𝑑x\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}\,\log\left(\frac{1}{\pi\,e}\,\frac{\left\|{\nabla u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\right)\geq\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,\log\left(\frac{|u|^{2}}{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\right)}\,dx (13)

for any function u∈H1​(ℝ2,d​x)u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2},dx), that can be found in [40, Theorem 2], [37, Inequality (2.3)], [19, Appendix B] or [9, Inequality (26)]. See [38, 26] for further references and consequences. Of course, (11) can be deduced from (13), so that (10), (11) and (13) are equivalent, and none of these inequalities is limited to d=2d=2, but constants in (11) and (13) have to be adapted to the dimension if d≠2d\neq 2.

It is possible to combine (3) and (11) with ρ=|u|2\rho=|u|^{2} into

∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x≥2​π‖u‖22​∫ℝ2|u|2​(−Δ)−1​|u|2​𝑑x+12​log⁡(2​e)​‖u‖22\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx\geq\frac{2\,\pi}{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}}\,dx+\frac{1}{2}\,\log(2\,e)\,\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2} (14)

where

2π∫ℝ2|u|2(−Δ)−1|u|2dx=−∬ℝ2×ℝ2|u(x)|2log|x−y||u(y)|2dy.2\,\pi\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}}\,dx=-\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}|u(x)|^{2}\,\log|x-y|\,|u(y)|^{2}\,dy\,.

By applying (14) to the scaled function uλ​(x)=λ​u​(λ​x)u_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda\,u(\lambda\,x), we obtain that

λ2​∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x−‖u‖22​log⁡λ≥2​π‖u‖22​∫ℝ2|u|2​(−Δ)−1​|u|2​𝑑x+12​log⁡(2​e)​‖u‖22\lambda^{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx-\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}\,\log\lambda\geq\frac{2\,\pi}{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}}\,dx+\frac{1}{2}\,\log(2\,e)\,\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2} (15)

for any λ>0\lambda>0. By optimizing on λ\lambda, we obtain the following scale invariant inequality.

Proposition 9.

For any function u∈H1​(ℝ2)u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), we have

2​π​∫ℝ2|u|2​(−Δ)−1​|u|2​𝑑x≤‖u‖24​log⁡(‖∇u‖2‖u‖2).2\,\pi\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}}\,dx\leq\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{4}\,\log\left(\frac{\left\|{\nabla u}\right\|_{2}}{\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}}\right)\,. (16)

Since (3) and (11) admit incompatible optimal functions, respectively the function ρ=ρ⋆\rho=\rho_{\star} given by (4) and the Gaussian function u(x)=(2π)−1/2Me−|x|2/4=M​μ​(x)u(x)=(2\,\pi)^{-1/2}\,\sqrt{M}\,e^{-|x|^{2}/4}=\sqrt{M\,\mu(x)}, up to multiplications by a constant, scalings and translations, equality is not achieved in (16) by a function u∈H1​(ℝ2)u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}).

3.2. Interpolations inequalities in higher dimensions

For comparison, let us briefly consider the case of higher dimensions, that is, the case of the Euclidean space ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} with d≥3d\geq 3. We can refer for instance to [3] for more detailed considerations on scalings in absence of an external potential. The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality

𝒞GN​‖∇u‖2ϑ​‖u‖21−ϑ≥‖u‖p∀u∈H1​(ℝd)\mathcal{C}_{\rm GN}\,\left\|{\nabla u}\right\|_{2}^{\vartheta}\,\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{1-\vartheta}\geq\left\|{u}\right\|_{p}\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{d}) (17)

holds with θ=d​p−22​p\theta=d\,\frac{p-2}{2\,p} for any p∈(2,2∗]p\in(2,2^{*}], where 2∗=2​dd−22^{*}=\frac{2\,d}{d-2} is the critical Sobolev exponent. Optimality is attained by the so-called Lommel functions, which are radial functions according to, e.g., [39], and are defined by the Euler-Lagrange but have no explicit formulation in terms of the usual special functions: see [31, 32]. This can be combined with the critical Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality,

1(d−2)​|𝕊d−1|​∬ℝd×ℝdρ⁡(x)​ρ​(y)|x−y|d−2​𝑑x​𝑑y=∫ℝdρ​(−Δ)−1​ρ​𝑑x≤𝒞HLS​(∫ℝd|ρ|2​dd+2​𝑑x)1+2d\frac{1}{(d-2)\,|\mathbb{S}^{d-1}|}\iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\frac{\rho(x)\,\rho(y)}{|x-y|^{d-2}}\,dx\,dy=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{\rho\,(-\Delta)^{-1}\rho}\,dx\leq\mathcal{C}_{\rm{HLS}}\left(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{|\rho|^{\frac{2\,d}{d+2}}}\,dx\right)^{1+\frac{2}{d}} (18)

for any function ρ∈L2​dd+2​(ℝd)\rho\in\mathrm{L}^{\frac{2\,d}{d+2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{d}), to establish for ρ=|u|2\rho=|u|^{2} that

𝒞d​∫ℝd|u|2​(−Δ)−1​|u|2​𝑑x≤‖∇u‖2d−2​‖u‖26−d∀u∈H1​(ℝd),\mathcal{C}_{d}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}}\,dx\leq\left\|{\nabla u}\right\|_{2}^{d-2}\,\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{6-d}\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{d})\,, (19)

under the condition that 4​dd+2≤2​dd−2\frac{4\,d}{d+2}\leq\frac{2\,d}{d-2}, that is, for

3≤d≤6.3\leq d\leq 6\,.

Let us notice that the inequality is critical if d=6d=6 in the sense that ∫ℝ6|u|2​(−Δ)−1​|u|2​𝑑x\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{6}}|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}\,dx and (∫ℝ6|∇u|2​𝑑x)2\left(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{6}}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx\right)^{2} have the same homogeneity and scaling invariance, which is a standard source of loss of compactness along an arbitrary minimizing sequence satisfying a given ‖u‖2\left\|{u}\right\|_{2} constraint. From (17) and (18), we find out that

𝒞d≥𝒞GN−4​𝒞HLS−1.\mathcal{C}_{d}\geq\mathcal{C}_{\rm{GN}}^{-4}\,\mathcal{C}_{\rm{HLS}}^{-1}\,.

The above estimate is strict because optimal functions do not coincide in (17) and (18) if 3≤d≤53\leq d\leq 5. In dimension d=6d=6, we have that 𝒞6=𝒞GN−4​𝒞HLS−1\mathcal{C}_{6}=\mathcal{C}_{\rm{GN}}^{-4}\,\mathcal{C}_{\rm{HLS}}^{-1} is sharp, with equality in (19) achieved by the Aubin-Talenti function x↦(1+|x|2)−2x\mapsto(1+|x|^{2})^{-2}.

3.3. Bounds on the Schrödinger energy

Let γ+:=max⁡{γ,0}\gamma_{+}:=\max\{\gamma,0\} and consider ℰ\mathcal{E} as in (1).

Theorem 10.

Let α\alpha, β\beta, γ\gamma be real parameters and assume that M>0M>0. Then

  1. (i)

    ℰ\mathcal{E} is not bounded from below on ℋM\mathcal{H}_{M} if one of the following conditions is satisfied:

    (a)\displaystyle\mathrm{(a)}\hskip 10.00002pt α<0,\displaystyle\alpha<0\,,
    (b)\displaystyle\mathrm{(b)}\hskip 10.00002pt α≥0andM​β>min⁡{2​α−γ,4​α−2​γ}.\displaystyle\alpha\geq 0\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002ptM\,\beta>\min\big\{2\,\alpha-\gamma,4\,\alpha-2\,\gamma\big\}\,.
  2. (ii)

    ℰ\mathcal{E} is bounded from below on ℋM\mathcal{H}_{M} if either α=0\alpha=0, β≤0\beta\leq 0 and M​β+2​γ≤0M\,\beta+2\,\gamma\leq 0, or α>0\alpha>0 and one of the following conditions is satisfied:

    (a)\displaystyle\mathrm{(a)}\hskip 10.00002pt γ≤0andM​β≤2​α,\displaystyle\gamma\leq 0\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002ptM\,\beta\leq 2\,\alpha\,,
    (b)\displaystyle\mathrm{(b)}\hskip 10.00002pt γ>0,Mβ≤4α−2γandMβ<2α−γ.\displaystyle\gamma>0\,,\hskip 10.00002ptM\,\beta\leq 4\,\alpha-2\,\gamma\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002ptM\,\beta<2\,\alpha-\gamma\,.

Two cases covered by Theorem 10 are shown in Fig. 2.

Proof.

Let us start by the proof of (i), i.e., the cases for which inf{ℰ⁡[u]:u∈ℋM}=−∞\inf\{\mathcal{E}[u]\,:\,u\in\mathcal{H}_{M}\}=-\infty. Case (a) corresponds to α<0\alpha<0 and can be dealt with using translations as in the proof of Lemma 5: lim|x0|→+∞ℰ[u(⋅−x0)]=−∞\lim_{|x_{0}|\to+\infty}\mathcal{E}[u(\cdot-x_{0})]=-\infty. Next let uλ​(x):=λ​u​(λ​x)u_{\lambda}(x):=\lambda\,u(\lambda\,x) and notice that

∫ℝ2|∇uλ|2​𝑑x=λ2​∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x=o⁡(log⁡λ)asλ→0+,\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u_{\lambda}|^{2}}\,dx=\lambda^{2}\,\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx=o(\log\lambda)\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{as}\hskip 10.00002pt\lambda\to 0_{+}\,,

so that, with ρλ=|uλ|2\rho_{\lambda}=|u_{\lambda}|^{2},

ℰ⁡[uλ]∼2​α​∫ℝ2log⁡(1+|x|2)​ρλ​𝑑x+2​π​β​∫ℝ2ρλ​(−Δ)−1​ρλ​𝑑x+γ​∫ℝ2ρλ​log​ρλ​𝑑x.\mathcal{E}[u_{\lambda}]\sim 2\,\alpha\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\log\left(1+|x|^{2}\right)\rho_{\lambda}}\,dx+2\,\pi\,\beta\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho_{\lambda}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}\rho_{\lambda}}\,dx+\gamma\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\rho_{\lambda}\,\log\rho_{\lambda}}\,dx\,.

By arguing as in Lemma 5, we obtain that limλ→0+ℰ⁡[uλ]=−∞\lim_{\lambda\to 0_{+}}\mathcal{E}[u_{\lambda}]=-\infty in case (b).

Concerning (ii), the boundedness from below of ℰ\mathcal{E} is as follows. From (12) and (15), we learn that

∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x≥12​λ12​∫ℝ2|u|2​log⁡(|u|2M)​𝑑x+log⁡(2​π​e2​λ12)2​λ12​M\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx\geq\frac{1}{2\,\lambda_{1}^{2}}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,\log\left(\frac{|u|^{2}}{M}\right)}\,dx+\frac{\log\left(2\,\pi\,e^{2}\,\lambda_{1}^{2}\right)}{2\,\lambda_{1}^{2}}\,M (20)

and

∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x≥2​πM​λ22​∫ℝ2|u|2​(−Δ)−1​|u|2​𝑑x+log⁡(2​e​λ22)2​λ22​M\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx\geq\frac{2\,\pi}{M\,\lambda_{2}^{2}}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}}\,dx+\frac{\log\left(2\,e\,\lambda_{2}^{2}\right)}{2\,\lambda_{2}^{2}}\,M (21)

with ‖u‖22=M\left\|{u}\right\|_{2}^{2}=M. Here λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} are two arbitrary positive parameters. Let us distinguish various cases:

  1. (1)

    If α=0\alpha=0, β≤0\beta\leq 0 and γ≤0\gamma\leq 0, the boundedness from below of ℰ\mathcal{E} is a direct consequence of (20) and (21). The case α=0\alpha=0, β<0\beta<0 and γ>0\gamma>0 can be reduced to the case α=0\alpha=0 and γ=0\gamma=0 using (3) if M​β+2​γ≤0M\,\beta+2\,\gamma\leq 0.

  2. (2)

    If either α>0\alpha>0, β≤0\beta\leq 0 and γ≤0\gamma\leq 0, or α>0\alpha>0, β>0\beta>0, γ≤0\gamma\leq 0 and M​β+2​γ≤0M\,\beta+2\,\gamma\leq 0, we conclude as above.

  3. (3)

    If α>0\alpha>0, β>0\beta>0 and γ≤0\gamma\leq 0, the boundedness from below is a direct consequence of Lemma 1 if M​β−2​α≤0M\,\beta-2\,\alpha\leq 0.

  4. (4)

    If α>0\alpha>0, γ>0\gamma>0 and M​β+2​γ≥0M\,\beta+2\,\gamma\geq 0, we notice that ℰ⁡[u]≥γ​ℱ𝖺,𝖻​[|u|2]\mathcal{E}[u]\geq\gamma\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}}\big[|u|^{2}\big] with 𝖺=2​α/γ\mathsf{a}=2\,\alpha/\gamma and 𝖻=M​β/γ\mathsf{b}=M\,\beta/\gamma. The result of Lemma 4 applies and the condition 𝖻<min⁡{𝖺−1,2​𝖺−2}\mathsf{b}<\min\{\mathsf{a}-1,2\,\mathsf{a}-2\} can be rewritten as M​β<min⁡{2​α−γ,4​α−2​γ}M\,\beta<\min\big\{2\,\alpha-\gamma,4\,\alpha-2\,\gamma\big\}. The case M​β=4​α−2​γM\,\beta=4\,\alpha-2\,\gamma corresponds to 𝖻=2​𝖺−2\mathsf{b}=2\,\mathsf{a}-2 and it is covered by Lemmas 6 and 7.

  5. (5)

    If α>0\alpha>0, γ>0\gamma>0 and M​β+2​γ<0M\,\beta+2\,\gamma<0, we conclude by observing that

    ℰ⁡[u]≥γ​ℱ𝖺,−2​[|u|2]+∫ℝ2|∇u|2​𝑑x+2​πM​(M​β+2​γ)​∫ℝ2|u|2​(−Δ)−1​|u|2​𝑑x,\mathcal{E}[u]\geq\gamma\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},-2}\big[\,|u|^{2}\,\big]+\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\,dx+\frac{2\,\pi}{M}\,(M\,\beta+2\,\gamma)\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{|u|^{2}\,(-\Delta)^{-1}|u|^{2}}\,dx\,,

    where, because M​β+2​γ<0M\,\beta+2\,\gamma<0, the sum of the last two terms is bounded from below in view (21) and where Lemma 4 guarantees that ℱ𝖺,−2​[|u|2]\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{a},-2}\big[\,|u|^{2}\,\big] is bounded from below.
